A family couch game for the big TV. Daddy, Abbie and Ani fly the pink rocket to the Moon base, together, out loud. Part 1 (tonight, after ballet): launch morning, the launch itself, the landing, and arriving at the Moon base.

Identity record: moon-mission.identity.json (schema 1.1). Story source: Evan's trek pack ("Abbie and Daddy's Moon Mission", /mnt/project-files/trek.zip). Heroes and buggy art: AW-STUDY-0029 Moon Heroes. Base environment: AW-STUDY-0031 Moon Base Kit. Voices: AW-STUDY-0030 Family cast.

2. The shape of the whole game

Act Name Games Ends with
1 Launch Morning (Part 1, tonight) the rocket tile, mission cards, Daddy's choices, three get-ready jobs, the crew bus, whiteboard training, Game 1 Launch, Game 2 Lunar Lander the lander's feet touch the pad outside the Moon base; Daddy's memory key
2 The Base Game 3 Wire Puzzle (the relays), Game 4 Bug Zapper (the gem bugs), Game 5 Star Child Harmonizer the Star Child hatches and sings with you
3 Home Game 6 Buggy Ride Home the buggy rolls into the hangar; the family photo

It's one evening per act. Each act is 30-45 minutes and stops at a cosy place.

3. How a family plays it on one TV

Who plays. Daddy plays Daddy. Abbie and Ani play themselves. A fourth seat (Mommy, a friend) can join as Flight Engineer at any time. Everyone is in the same rocket. The camera is first person from whoever has the spotlight, and the others are seen beside them in their seats.

Jobs, not turns. Every beat gives each person a job they own, and the beat can't go on without them. The jobs are physical and loud, and each one is a six-year-old's important job: - Abbie: Oxygen Officer (plug in the oxygen, check the green lights, seal the helmets). - Ani: Lights and Radio Officer (cabin lights, the radio, and saying "Roger!" to Houston). - Daddy: Commander (the checklist, the big arm switch, and flying the lander). - Guest: Flight Engineer (fuel, the countdown clock, the snack pack). A job is a key on the capsule panel (the Stream Deck) or a button on your own pad. The key shows the job's picture.

Group choices. When the story forks, everyone votes by pressing. Each choice is a line beneath the thought (>), with a small glowing chip on it for each vote, coloured by person (pink Abbie, purple Ani, blue Daddy, green Engineer). - A majority wins after three seconds. - If it's a tie, the Captain's Hat decides. The hat is a real object that travels with the crew, and it moves to a new person after every choice, so everyone gets to be the decider. - Some choices belong to one person: their face lights up and only their button counts ("Ani, it's your patch!").

Group dynamics, made fun: - Cheering: holding all buttons together does a "together" move (the cabin cheers, Houston notices). - Helping hands: if a job is waiting more than 8 seconds, its key starts to pulse and another person can "help". Both get the credit. - No one fails alone. A miss is shared and funny ("Oops, that was the snack button!"), never one child's fault.

Lots of text, readable from the sofa. Every line is on screen in big type (TV-safe, 48 px at 1080p, at most two lines) and also spoken in the character's own voice, because six-year-olds can't read it all yet. Reading along with the voice is part of the fun. Captions sit on the bottom edge like the basement's inner voice, in the Moon dialect: white on a thin dark glass bar, with the speaker's colour as a dot.

4. Talking, chatting and branching dialogue

The grammar is docs/design/INTERACTION_GRAMMAR.md rules 7-8: a thought or line, then > choices beneath.

  • Branching dialogue. Scripted scenes are a small graph in moon-mission/script.json: each node is a line (who, text, voice line id), its choices, what each choice sets (flags) and where it goes. A choice can change a later line, an item you carry, or which side quest opens.
  • Chat with characters. At rest moments (breakfast, the suit workshop, orbit, the base canteen) you can tap any character to talk. You get three or four chat topics as > lines ("Are you scared?", "What's on the Moon?", "Tell me about Grace"). These are scripted. Houston, and later the Star Child, can also answer freely, live (section 6).
  • Lines remember. Characters bring up earlier choices ("You picked the purple patch! Good choice, Lieutenant.").

5. Inventory and crafting

The shared player inventory (simulations/inventory.mjs) holds what the crew carries. Each item says who found it.

Crafting is building your suit (Get ready 1) and Ani's meal plan (Get ready 2), and later fixing things at the base. A recipe is parts laid on the workbench:

Recipe Parts Makes
Space suit suit body + gloves + boots + chest pack your suit (colour = you)
Helmet helmet shell + visor + light your helmet
Mission patch patch blank + a drawing stamp your patch (it shows on the suit all game)
Oxygen pack canister + hose + clip plugs into the seat
Snack pack (Ani's meal plan) one thing from each colour shelf + a sticker one per crew member, shared in orbit
Glow wand (Act 2) glow stick + crystal shard it lights the dark tunnel at the base
Bug net (Act 2) net + pole + crystal the bug zapper's tool

Starting items: the toy rocket (Abbie), the old radio (Daddy, from Grace's basement), a star map (Ani), crayons.

6. Houston: live launch control by voice

Houston is a real-time voice on the capsule radio. The family talks to it out loud, and it answers in its own designed voice. "We HAVE TO GET IT RIGHT", so this section is the heart of Part 1.

How it works (reusing what is live): - The brain is the live-mode relay (api/live.js ticket, then api/live-socket.js to the realtime model), with a new houston policy: its own instructions, its own small tool set, and the same PG and jailbreak guard. Its speaking voice is a designed ElevenLabs voice (houston in tools/voice-cast/cast.json), streamed live with api/live-voice.js. - Push to talk, like a real radio. Hold the RADIO key on the panel (or a pad's shoulder button) to talk. A radio click and hiss starts and stops it. This keeps the TV's sound out of the mic and makes turn-taking feel real. - Houston runs the launch script, and improvises around it. The script is the spine: every callout and every job happens in order. Houston's tools are job_done(job), next_step(), hold(reason), say_line(id) and cheer(). The game state is the truth: Houston can never skip a job, and it gets each step's state from the game. - It must sound right. It uses real launch-control rhythm, in kid words: the poll ("Oxygen?" "GO!" "Lights?" "GO!"), "T minus 10", "main engines starting", "liftoff!", "you're clear of the tower", "engine cut-off", "stage separation", "welcome to space, Moon Rocket". - It answers anything kind. "Houston, can we bring bub?" gets a warm answer and a reason. Off-topic or unkind things get steered back to the mission in one line. - If the network fails, Houston plays its pre-rendered lines and the jobs still work with buttons. Nobody waits.

Before tonight (safety and cost): - The realtime model will hear children's voices. Live mode's open item applies: confirm the provider runs with zero data retention for this, or keep the kids' talk to push-to-talk in Daddy's hand tonight. Evan decides (section 13). - Every paid call goes through wallet().charge (the AI caps). A 40-minute launch evening costs well under the $1000 owner cap.

7. The six games

Each game has a design card (abbies-world-designer skill).

The rocket tile (the way in)

  • The pink rocket is a special hex tile in the hand. You drop it like any tile (the piece-fall from simulations/tile-drop-impact.mjs), and a beat later the rocket itself falls onto it from the sky, lands on its feet with a puff of dust and a "clunk-hiss", and stands there humming. Tapping it opens Moon Mission.
  • Card: Know: "a rocket is here and it's ours". How would the character know: it lands, steams and its hatch light blinks. Mode: diegetic. Adapts: lights on the ranch turn to look at it; sheep stare.

Game 1: Launch (Act 1)

Launch morning (cards, get-ready jobs, choices, the crew bus, whiteboard training), then the launch. Full script in section 8. - Card: Feel: "We're really doing it. My job matters. LIFTOFF!" How would the characters know: Houston's voice, the panel lights, the seat shaking, the sky going dark blue then black. Mode: diegetic (panel, voice, window), meta (rumble, heartbeat, the music swelling), spatial (each person's job glow on their seat). Adapts: one signal, the countdown, drives light, sound, shake and music together.

Game 2: Lunar Lander (Act 1)

Daddy flies; the girls spot. A first-person cockpit with a window and the PIP screen (the picture-in-picture camera under the lander, which is what we showcase). The girls call out what they see on the PIP ("Rock! Go left!"). - The rule is simple and the world shows it: falling too fast makes the alarm light blink and the ground rush up. Soft landing = a gentle bump and a cheer. - Daddy holds the stick (left stick = tilt, trigger = thrust). Abbie's job: the landing lights. Ani's job: the "feet down" switch. The landing can't finish until both are done. - Nothing fails: a hard landing is a big bounce and Houston laughing "Well, you're down!". Points for gentle. - Reward: Daddy's memory key (the Moon base is a core memory), golden reward from coin-reward.mjs.

Game 3: Wire Puzzle (Act 2)

From the trek pack's electrical puzzle. Daddy opens the relay box; the girls each hold one colour of wire and connect it on the TV. Light flows when it's right.

Game 4: Bug Zapper (Act 2)

From gem bugs swat. Gem bugs swarm the crystals. Each player has a crystal zapper and their own colour of sparkle. Bugs aren't hurt: zapped bugs turn into glitter and float away happy.

Game 5: Star Child Harmonizer (Act 2)

From the signal lock game. The meteorite hums a tune. Each player holds one note (one button). Together you match its song, and the Star Child hatches. Its chat is live (the second live voice), gentle and curious.

Game 6: Buggy Ride Home (Act 3)

Daddy drives the buggy (in its fine parts, AW-STUDY-0029). The girls are passengers with jobs: the horn, the headlights, the radio song. A calm ride through the waypoints, with Earth rising.

8. Act 1 in detail: Launch Morning

The reference (style, never expression). Deliver Us Mars opens with a quiet family moment, then a first-person launch day: you walk through the place you'll leave, put your hands on a real-feeling cockpit, work the checklist with launch control in your ear, and feel the launch in your body, then the hush of orbit. We take that rhythm: quiet home, tactile cockpit, a voice in your ear, the roar, then silence and the window. We don't take its story, characters, ship or music.

The opening: the black truck (4 min, everyone)

HOUSTON BASECAMP · T-24:00:00 · MAIN STREET, ABBIE'S TOWN (the clock isn't running yet; it starts at the stamp). This is the first scene, and the only one that starts in the town, at the coffee shop. 1. The truck. A quiet morning outside the coffee shop. A long, glossy black truck rolls up Main Street and parks at the curb with a low hum (its engine is the same sound the crew bus will have later, so the ear remembers it). It's very important and knows it: tinted glass, a small pink antenna light, a plain white patch on the door. Bub sits up. People on the street stop and look (spatial cue: the whole street turns toward it). 2. The offer. A person in a crisp suit steps out (a mission officer; a designed voice, never a clone) and walks to the family's table. First person, from whoever has the spotlight (Daddy first). The offer is a short branching chat, a few > lines, each person with their own question: - Daddy: > "A mission? To where?" or > "Is this a joke?" - Abbie: > "Is it a really big rocket?" or > "Can Ani come?" - Ani: > "Can we bring snacks?" or > "Will there be stars?" The officer answers each, then opens a folder: a mission patch, a star map, and a pink rocket drawn by a child. "The Moon base needs a crew. A very important one." 3. And we accept. The family accepts together: this is the first group moment. The question is one line, > We accept, and everyone has to say yes: by voice ("We accept!", heard on the room mic as a loud group shout) or by each player pressing their own button. Each yes puts a glowing chip (pink, purple, blue) on the line; when all chips are lit the officer stamps the folder. The group can't be outvoted: if someone hesitates, the officer waits kindly ("Take your time, crew."), and the clock does not tick yet. The mission clock starts at this stamp. 4. KABOOM. The truck's rear door drops to show a glowing pad outside it, and then, from above, a huge rocket port lands: a launch platform drops onto Main Street and plants itself with a ring of dust and a low boom. A beat later the pink rocket appears on it, kaboom: a burst of light, a shock ring, confetti-like sparks, the rocket standing on the pad, steaming, its hatch light blinking. The street gasps and cheers. - It's the same beat as the rocket tile landing on the Ranch (section 7), seen from the ground: the port's drop reuses the tile-drop impact (simulations/tile-drop-impact.mjs), and the pink ship's appearance reuses a reveal effect from the Tile pull and print study (simulations/live-tray-preview.mjs reveal, the five effects in AW-STUDY-0025; we pick the same one Evan picks there, or the biggest by default). Nothing in the world masks the view: no white flash fade, the burst is light and sparks on the rocket itself. - Meta cues: a low boom in the chest, a short camera shake, the coffee cups on the table rattle and settle. - Daddy's thought: "Well. That's a big rocket." 5. Cut to the morning. A calm cutscene: the sun going down on the pink rocket on Main Street, the town settling, then the mission card for the next scene types in: T-00:45:00 · THE KITCHEN. The morning vignettes begin. - Where it lives: the coffee shop is placed at its real Main Street spot by the Abbie's Town thread (AW-STUDY-0033, Founding City on Hexes). The truck's arrival point is the curb in front of the shop's door and its trigger is "the family sits down at the shop's table" (or taps the shop door). Asked of that thread (not yet confirmed): expose the shop's curb position and door as named anchors; this study owns the truck, the officer, the port and the reveal. - Assets (added to section 10): the black truck, the mission officer, the folder and patch, the launch port (platform and dust ring), the kaboom effect, the street crowd reactions, and the Main Street backdrop from the town.

Mission cards (between scenes)

Evan (13:15Z): "a kind of high resolution mission update overlay that you'd see in movies". Every scene opens with one:

HOUSTON BASECAMP · T-00:30:00 · ABBIE'S TREE HOUSE

  • Where it sits in the grammar: overlay, "only you know", precise information (place, mission clock, whose scene). Play itself stays wordless; the card lives in the gap between scenes, like a film's location super, and is gone before you can act. It never covers play and never masks the world (no dimming, no blur).
  • Look: the one razor-sharp layer in a warm, soft game. A thin monospaced line, typed in letter by letter with a quiet teletype tick, a hairline underline drawing left to right, the mission clock ticking live. Bottom-left third, about 3% of the screen, 3 seconds, then it types itself away.
  • The launch clock is always ticking. From the first scene, a real mission clock counts down to launch in real time: on the cards, on the kitchen oven clock, on the bus dashboard, on the pad's big board, on the capsule panel. Nothing fails because of it: like a real launch it has planned holds. If the crew needs more time, Houston calls "We're holding at T minus 20" and the clock waits, with a calm music bed, until the crew is ready.
  • Calm cutscenes between scenes. Every change of scene is a slow, quiet 8-15 second cutscene: a long camera move (the tree house at sunrise, the rocket steaming on the pad, the bus on the road), ambient sound and the morning theme, and the mission card typing in over it. It can be skipped once everyone holds their button.
  • Reuse: simulations/mission-card.mjs in the couch kit (missionCard({org, clock, place, who})).

Cold open: Daddy's two choices (3 min)

HOUSTON BASECAMP · T-00:45:00 · THE KITCHEN. Dawn, first person as Daddy, coffee, the pink rocket through the window, bub at his heels. - Choice 1, how the day starts: > Wake them early for the sunrise on the rocket (sets sunrise: the launch is golden) or > Let them sleep and make Moon pancakes (sets pancakes: they go in the meal plan). - Choice 2, the one thing Daddy brings: > Grace's old radio (sets radio: a song from home in orbit) or > Bub's chewed toy rocket (sets bubrocket: a dashboard mascot; bub howls at liftoff).

Get ready 1: Abbie's suit (group activity, 8 min)

HOUSTON BASECAMP · T-00:30:00 · ABBIE'S TREE HOUSE. Abbie: "What should I wear? I'll never be ready for launch if I don't have my space suit... Ani, will you help me get ready?" - > "Of course!" / > "Only if I get to pick the helmet light!" (Ani's pick, her button only). - Group crafting on one bench: Abbie picks the parts, Ani hands them over and does the fiddly bits (zips, clips, the glove seals). Each part needs both: one picks, one fastens. Abbie draws her mission patch. - Side quest: one glove is missing (bub has it).

Get ready 2: Ani's meal plan (6 min)

HOUSTON BASECAMP · T-00:20:00 · THE GALLEY. Ani: "I have to prep the meal plans for the trip, so we're nourished." - Crafting: Ani builds a snack pack for each crew member from a pantry shelf (crackers, juice, fruit, Moon pancakes if pancakes). Each crew member says what they like, and Abbie can call out requests. A good pack has something from each colour shelf (a plate-of-colours rule, shown by the tray filling with colour, never a number). - Packs go into the inventory and come out in orbit (a shared snack scene).

Get ready 3: Daddy's flight check (6 min)

HOUSTON BASECAMP · T-00:12:00 · THE PAD. Daddy walks around the rocket with the inspection clipboard: fins, engines, hatch, oxygen line, landing light, the stage ring. Each point is a close-up. - Three things are wrong: dirt or oil on a window (wipe it), a disconnected plug on the oxygen line, a loose panel cap. Daddy finds them; the girls fix them ("Abbie, can you plug that back in?"), each on their own button. - The clipboard gets a tick for each point. Missing a problem is fine: Houston catches it later in the poll and it becomes a fun extra job.

The girls' morning choices (3 min)

HOUSTON BASECAMP · T-00:08:00 · THE DRIVEWAY - Abbie: > Bring my toy rocket for luck or > Bring a drawing for the Moon base wall. - Ani: > Bring the star map or > Bring a harmonica (it comes back in Game 5, the Star Child Harmonizer).

The crew bus: "Wake up, sleepy heads!" (2 min)

HOUSTON BASECAMP · T-00:06:00 · THE CREW BUS. The calm cutscene shows the three of them climbing into the crew bus in their white suits and dozing off against the windows. Then, in first person: the bus engine turns over, muffled, as if heard through sleep; the eyelids open in two slow blinks (the player's own eyes, a meta beat, not a screen fade); the sound comes clear; the pink rocket is huge through the windscreen. Houston on the bus radio:

"Wake up, sleepy heads! I know you three have been working hard for today, so I hope you enjoyed a little shut-eye. Now it's time to get ready for our launch sequence." The bus pulls up at the training building. Free chat: tap anyone to talk.

Training: the whiteboard briefing (5 min)

HOUSTON BASECAMP · T-00:05:00 · CREW BRIEFING ROOM. A real whiteboard in a briefing room. Houston explains the launch, and the steps draw themselves on the board stroke by stroke, like a child's marker drawing: the rocket, four stick figures in seats, a hose going into a seat ("Abbie plugs in the oxygen"), a light bulb ("Ani turns on the launch lights"), a lever ("Daddy pulls ARM"), the countdown, a big whoosh. - Procedural, never generated images. Each picture is a small list of strokes (lines, arcs, loops) drawn by a procedure that moves a marker tip along them at hand speed with a slight wobble, with a marker squeak sound. Words are written the same way in a hand-drawn font, assembled stroke by stroke (single-line font outlines, revealed along the path). Evan: "do not tokenize the drawing of characters on a whiteboard in a video game, let a procedure do that." - Each kid's figure is drawn in their marker colour (pink, purple, blue), and the rocket is drawn in pink. The board stays on the wall, and Houston can point back at it in the launch ("Remember the hose picture?"). - Reuse: simulations/whiteboard.mjs (board.draw(strokes, {color, speed}), board.write(text, {font})), with a small stroke library (rocket, stick figure, seat, hose, bulb, lever, arrow, star, Moon). - Ends: "Any questions, crew?" (a free chat with Houston), then the walk-out: elevator up the gantry, white room, climbing into four seats, the hatch thunk, and the first radio call: "Moon Rocket, this is Houston. Good morning, crew."

The launch (10-15 min, everyone, live Houston)

Houston runs it; every job must be done by its owner (hold the RADIO key to talk back): 1. Radio check. Each person says their name and "loud and clear". (Ani's job: "Roger!") 2. "PLUG IN OUR OXYGEN!!!" (Abbie). Her key shows the hose; pressing it clicks the hose in, a green light comes on, and the suit hiss starts. 3. Helmets on, visors down (each person presses their own; a seal sound and the view gets a thin visor edge). 4. Cabin lights to launch mode (Ani). The cabin goes from white to a red-and-blue glow. 5. Fuel full (Engineer or Daddy), the fuel gauge fills on the panel. 6. The poll. Houston calls each job and each owner shouts "GO!" (the mic hears it, or press GO). 7. Daddy's big ARM switch, under a flip cover. 8. T minus 10. Everyone counts down with Houston. Rumble begins at 5, main engines at 3. 9. LIFTOFF. The seat shakes, the sky through the window goes from blue to deep blue to black, the music swells, Houston: "Liftoff! You're clear of the tower!" Bub howls at home (if bubrocket). 10. Engine cut-off, stage separation (a big clunk), silence, and floating crayons. "Welcome to space, Moon Rocket." 11. Orbit rest stop: share the snack pack, look at Earth, the radio song (if radio), chat with Houston freely.

Game 2 then: to the Moon base

Transfer is a short cutscene (the Moon growing in the window, a sleepy "are we there yet" chat). Then the lander separates and Game 2 begins. Part 1 ends when the lander touches down on the base's pad, the airlock lights blink on, and Daddy gets the golden key: "This place... I've been here before. In a memory."

9. Art direction (part of this design)

Folded in from the AW-STUDY-0029 Faceted Hero direction, with Evan's changes of 13:17Z. Where they differ, this wins for Moon Mission.

One line: Earth is light mode, the Moon is dark mode, and the pink rocket carries you from one to the other.

  1. Light mode on Earth. Launch morning is bright and clean: white suits, white rooms, daylight, pale sky, soft shadows, with the crew's colours as accents. The kitchen, tree house, galley, pad and briefing room are daylight scenes.
  2. Dark mode on the Moon. After liftoff the sky goes deep blue, then black. On the Moon everything is dark mode: black sky, hard white sunlight, lit panels, glowing trim on the suits, the base's lights and holograms (the Moon dialect). The switch from light to dark IS the launch.
  3. White suits for everyone. Abbie, Ani and Daddy wear the same white suit with their colour as trim (Abbie pink, Ani purple, Daddy blue) on the patch, glove cuffs, helmet light and boot stripe. In dark mode the trim glows. Suits are fitted to the Meshy bodies by the accessorize kit.
  4. The pink rocket is the hero. Pink and white with a silver nose, round portholes and four fins; rounded and toy-like, but built like a real rocket (stage ring, engine bells, umbilical arm). It is in almost every shot: through the kitchen window, the tree house window, on the whiteboard, in the bus windscreen. It is also the hex tile.
  5. Characters are Faceted Heroes: Meshy bodies cleaned up, low-poly faceted, with real materials. Ani's skin #ddb08c; Daddy now (bald, salt-and-pepper beard).
  6. First person with hands. You see your own gloved hands with your colour on the cuff. FOV 70 degrees, a child's eye height for the girls and an adult's for Daddy. A small head bob when walking, none in the seat.
  7. Tactile panels. Every switch is big, chunky and labelled with a picture, not a word, with a guard, a light and a click. The same pictures are on the Stream Deck keys, so the panel on the TV and the panel on the table match.
  8. Light only from real things. Nothing masks the world: no haze, fade or blur. The eyelids on the bus are the one exception, and they are the player's own eyes in a cutscene.
  9. One high-resolution layer: the mission card. A crisp monospaced line in the cutscenes, dark ink in light mode and white in dark mode. It is the only sharp type, and its contrast with the soft world gives the movie feel.
  10. The whiteboard is a child's marker drawing made by a procedure, stroke by stroke.
  11. Sound on the grid. Diegetic: the radio, switches, hiss, engines, the bus. Meta: the heartbeat at T minus 5, the muffled wake-up, the music. Overlay: the card's teletype tick, very quiet.
  12. No HUD during play. The launch clock lives on things (the oven clock, the bus dashboard, the pad board, the capsule panel); the checklist is paper; jobs glow on their keys and seats; captions only at the bottom.

12. Home setup (the living room)

  • Mac M5 to the Frame by a USB-C to HDMI cable. AirPlay works but adds lag you feel on button timing.
  • Stream Deck on the coffee table = the capsule panel. Chrome talks to it over WebHID; each key shows the job's picture and lights up when it's that job's turn.
  • One 8BitDo pad per person (Bluetooth; the browser's Gamepad API needs no setup). Daddy's has a stick for the lander.
  • The Polycom = the capsule radio. Houston speaks from it and listens through it, and its echo cancelling keeps the TV out of the mic. Hold RADIO to talk.
  • Without any of it, the keyboard works: 1-4 are the players, Space is RADIO.

15. Context engineering

Evan (13:55Z, org-wide): every study lists the context it was built from. This is what fed Moon Mission, and what each source changed.

Oracle consultation (Game Oracle knowledge search, 2026-10-23 13:56Z, queries "couch co-op launch countdown family voice" and "space moon first person cockpit lander"): - Bluey: The Videogame (studied profile: "gentle, co-op, no fail; for preschoolers and parents together"). This confirmed the no-fail, parent-plus-kids model and the low challenge setting (0.11) for Act 1. - Overcooked! 2 (owned, installed): couch co-op where talking is the game. Kept: shared, shouted jobs. Left out: the time-pressure stress. - Deliver Us The Moon (owned, studied): KeokeN's earlier Moon game, with an atmospheric, slow tempo (0.22). It confirmed the calm cutscenes between scenes. - Kerbal Space Program (owned, studied): real launch vocabulary can be funny and educational at once. - The Abbie's World identity record: no fail screens, nothing masks the world, the world is the HUD. - Not run: the Oracle's model-written consult plan (it needs the server key from this session). It should be the first step of the next study.

Our canon: docs/oracle/identity/GAME_IDENTITY.md and its schema, docs/oracle/hud/HUD_STUDY.md, docs/design/INTERACTION_GRAMMAR.md, GAME_FEEL.md, the school and basement speed reviews, AW-STUDY-0029 Faceted Hero, AW-STUDY-0030 Family cast, AW-STUDY-0031 Moon Base Kit, and Evan's trek pack.

Game dev blogs and interviews: - First Deliver Us Mars dev diary and the interview with game director Koen Deetman. These gave the reference rhythm for the launch day (style only). - Everybody Shake! The Making of Spaceteam, chapter 2: split the panel so one person's instruction is another's job, teach less and let players discover, make teamwork the only way through, and let rising chaos make people shout. This became jobs, not turns and "PLUG IN OUR OXYGEN!!!". - The design principles behind Jackbox: minimal inputs, one task at a time, and pacing like a TV show with a host. This became Houston as host, one key per child, and the mission cards. - Ghost Town Games on Overcooked as "an evening thing": one act per evening.

Game design talks and tutorials: - GDC: Designing Asymmetric Gameplay for Keep Talking and Nobody Explodes: the information on the TV, the job pictures on the panel, and talking across the gap. This became the lander's spotters (the girls see the PIP camera, Daddy flies). - Built-in hold and Why the shuttle countdown has so many stops and starts: real countdowns pause on purpose. This became the always-ticking launch clock with planned holds, so nobody fails.

Context engineering

What this study was built from, and what each source changed.

Oracle consultation

  • Bluey: The Videogame: gentle, no-fail co-op for parents and kids, so Act 1 stays low-challenge.
  • Overcooked! 2: talking is the game. We keep the shouted jobs and drop the time stress.
  • Deliver Us The Moon: a slow, atmospheric tempo, so there's a calm cutscene between scenes.
  • Kerbal Space Program: real launch words can be funny and teach at the same time.
  • Abbie's World identity: no fail screens, and the world is the HUD.
  • Not run yet: the Oracle's written consult plan. It's first on the list for the next study.

Game dev blogs

  • The Making of Spaceteam: one person's instruction is another person's job. That's where "PLUG IN OUR OXYGEN!!!" comes from.
  • Jackbox design principles: one task at a time, paced like a TV show. Houston is the host.
  • Deliver Us Mars dev diary and Koen Deetman interview: the rhythm of launch day. We take the style only.
  • Ghost Town Games interview: "an evening thing", so it's one act per evening.

Game design talks and tutorials

  • GDC: asymmetric design in Keep Talking: the girls spot on the PIP camera while Daddy flies.
  • Built-in holds and Scientific American on countdowns: the clock always ticks, and planned holds mean nobody fails.

Our canon

Game identity schema, the HUD study, the interaction grammar, GAME_FEEL, the school and basement speed reviews, Faceted Hero, Family cast, the Moon Base Kit, and the trek pack.
